section.title: Saul Delivers Jabesh-gilead
section.sectionRationale: Saul's kingship is proved in action. Nahash the Ammonite besieges Jabesh-gilead and demands to gouge out every right eye. When the news reaches Saul at his plow, the Spirit of God rushes on him; he rallies all Israel, routs the Ammonites, and rescues the city. Saul refuses to take revenge on those who had doubted him, giving glory to the LORD who has worked salvation, and the kingship is joyfully renewed at Gilgal. It is one movement: the Spirit-empowered king delivers his people and is confirmed.
section.thesis: When Saul is moved by the Spirit of God, he becomes the deliverer Israel needed, saving Jabesh-gilead, crediting the victory to the LORD, and sparing his critics, so that at his best Saul shows what a king under God can be, a Spirit-filled saviour of his people, and points beyond himself to the King who saves for good.
section.frameNote: Four beats: Nahash's cruel siege of Jabesh, verses 1 to 4; the Spirit rushes on Saul and Israel rallies, verses 5 to 8; the rescue of Jabesh-gilead, verses 9 to 11; and mercy to critics and the kingship renewed, verses 12 to 15.

units.label: Nahash's cruel siege of Jabesh
units.note: that I may put out everyone's right eye

verses.text: Then Nahash the Ammonite came up and laid siege to Jabesh-gilead. All the men of Jabesh said to him, “Make a treaty with us, and we will serve you.”
But Nahash the Ammonite replied, “I will make a treaty with you on one condition, that I may put out everyone’s right eye and bring reproach upon all Israel.”
“Hold off for seven days,” replied the elders of Jabesh, “and let us send messengers throughout Israel. If there is no one to save us, we will surrender to you.”
When the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul and relayed these words in the hearing of the people, they all wept aloud.

units.label: The Spirit rushes on Saul and Israel rallies
units.note: the Spirit of God rushed upon him

verses.text: Just then Saul was returning from the field, behind his oxen. “What troubles the people?” asked Saul. “Why are they weeping?” And they relayed to him the words of the men from Jabesh.
When Saul heard their words, the {{ruach|Spirit of God}} rushed upon him, and he burned with great anger.

He took a pair of oxen, cut them into pieces, and sent them by messengers throughout the land of Israel, proclaiming, “This is what will be done to the oxen of anyone who does not march behind Saul and Samuel.” Then the {{pachad|terror of the LORD}} fell upon the people, and they came out together as one man.
And when Saul numbered them at Bezek, there were 300,000 Israelites and 30,000 men of Judah.

So they said to the messengers who had come, “Tell the men of Jabesh-gilead: ‘Deliverance will be yours tomorrow by the time the sun is hot.’” And when the messengers relayed this to the men of Jabesh, they rejoiced.
Then the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, “Tomorrow we will come out, and you can do with us whatever seems good to you.”

The next day Saul organized the troops into three divisions, and during the morning watch they invaded the camp of the Ammonites and slaughtered them, until the hottest part of the day. And the survivors were so scattered that no two of them were left together.

units.label: Mercy to critics and the kingship renewed
units.note: today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel

verses.text: Then the people said to Samuel, “Who said that Saul should not reign over us? Bring those men here so we can kill them!”
But Saul ordered, “No one shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked {{teshuah|salvation}} in Israel.”
Then Samuel said to the people, “Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there.”
So all the people went to Gilgal and confirmed Saul as king in the presence of the LORD. There they sacrificed peace offerings before the LORD, and Saul and all the Israelites rejoiced greatly.

ruach.gloss: Spirit, wind, breath. The Spirit of God rushes upon Saul as He did upon the judges, empowering him to rally Israel and deliver Jabesh. The same Spirit that came upon him at his anointing now moves him to act; the whole rescue is presented as the fruit of God's Spirit working through the king, not merely Saul's own resolve.

pachad.gloss: Dread, terror. The terror of the LORD, not merely fear of Saul, falls on the people so that they rally as one man. It is God who moves the nation to respond; the phrase credits the sudden unity and courage of Israel to the LORD, who stirs His people to the deliverance He is about to work.

teshuah.gloss: Salvation, deliverance, victory. Saul refuses revenge because today the LORD has worked teshuah in Israel; he names the rescue as God's saving act, not his own triumph. The word runs through Scripture for God's deliverance of His people, reaching its fullness in the salvation wrought by Jesus, whose very name means the LORD saves.

basic.context: Saul's kingship is tested at once. Nahash, king of the Ammonites, besieges the Israelite town of Jabesh-gilead and offers terms so cruel they are meant to humiliate all Israel: surrender, and I will gouge out every right eye. The desperate town sends for help. When the news reaches Saul, freshly returned from plowing, the Spirit of God rushes on him and he is filled with righteous anger. He summons all Israel with a dramatic call, and the terror of the LORD moves the people to come as one. Saul routs the Ammonites and saves Jabesh. When the crowd wants to kill those who had doubted him, Saul refuses, giving God the glory for the salvation. The kingship is joyfully renewed at Gilgal. The question is: what does a king under God look like? Here, at his best, Saul is a Spirit-filled deliverer who points the glory to the LORD.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative showing Saul at his finest, and it must be read in the flow of the book, which will soon show his decline. The rescue is genuinely good and genuinely God's work through the Spirit-empowered king. We should not simply extract Saul as a hero to imitate, nor ignore that this bright beginning makes his later failure all the more tragic. Its enduring truths are that God saves His people through appointed deliverers empowered by His Spirit, and that the right response to victory is humble praise, not revenge.
basic.originalLanguages: The rescue begins when the ruach, the Spirit of God, rushes on Saul as on the judges, moving him to act. The pachad, the terror of the LORD, not merely of Saul, falls on the people so they rally as one man; God Himself stirs the nation. And Saul names the outcome teshuah, salvation, the LORD has worked salvation in Israel, crediting the deliverance to God and refusing personal revenge.
basic.typology: Saul, empowered by the Spirit to deliver his people and then giving glory to God who worked salvation, is a shadow of the true Deliverer, the Spirit-anointed King who saves His people and gives all glory to the Father. The rescue of a doomed town under threat of blinding mutilation points to the greater salvation of a people doomed under the enemy, accomplished by Christ. Saul's mercy to his critics faintly reflects the King who prays for His enemies.
basic.christ: Saul says, today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel, and in that moment he is a picture of kingship as it should be, God saving His people through His anointed. But Saul's salvation is partial and passing, from one enemy on one day. Jesus, whose name means the LORD saves, is the true and final King who works salvation, not from Ammonites but from sin, death, and the devil, and not for a day but forever. Where Saul spared his critics in an hour of triumph, Christ, in His hour, prayed, Father, forgive them, and saved even His enemies. Saul at his best points to the Saviour who never fails.
basic.god: God is the true worker of salvation, moving through His Spirit-empowered king and stirring His people with holy dread to accomplish rescue. He is not distant from the suffering of a besieged town but raises up a deliverer in answer to their cry. He is the giver of victory, to whom the honor belongs. And He is patient, granting Israel a real deliverance through the king they demanded, confirming the throne in mercy.
basic.crossReferences: Judges 3 and 6 show the Spirit rushing on judges to deliver Israel, the pattern Saul follows. Exodus 14 declares that the salvation is the LORD's. Luke 23 records Christ praying for His enemies. And Matthew 1 gives the name Jesus, for He will save His people from their sins.
basic.oneStory: At his best, Saul is a Spirit-empowered king who saves his people and gives God the glory, showing what kingship under God can be. Yet his salvation is partial and his glory brief. The pattern points beyond him to Christ, the Spirit-anointed King whose name is salvation, who saves His people from their true enemies forever and gives all glory to God.

context.literary:
This chapter completes the account of Saul's rise, chapters 9 to 11, and vindicates the doubters of chapter 10 by showing Saul actually saving Israel. It parallels the judges: a threat, the Spirit's rushing, a rallying of the tribes, and deliverance. The renewal of the kingship at Gilgal, verses 14 to 15, closes the section on a high note before Samuel's farewell in chapter 12.

The chapter is built on the same four-beat pattern the book of Judges uses again and again, an enemy oppresses, Israel is in danger, the Spirit rushes on a chosen deliverer, and rescue follows, so that a first hearer recognizes the shape immediately even while watching it play out under a king rather than a judge. The blending is deliberate. Saul behaves exactly like Othniel or Gideon here, which is precisely the point the next chapter will need, since Samuel is about to argue that Israel already had judges enough to save them without asking for a king at all.

Saul's grim summons, cutting a pair of oxen into pieces and sending them through Israel with a threat, verse 7, deliberately recalls the one other time in Israel's story that pieces of a body were sent throughout the tribes to summon them, the concubine cut limb by limb into twelve pieces and sent throughout the territory of Israel after the atrocity at Gibeah, Judges 19:29. That earlier summons rallied Israel to civil war against Benjamin, nearly destroying the tribe. This summons, issued by a Benjamite king, rallies the same twelve tribes to rescue a city instead, and the echo turns a symbol of national horror into a symbol of national rescue.
context.historical:
The Ammonites lived east of the Jordan and pressed on Israelite territory there. Gouging out the right eye would cripple a man's ability to fight, since the left eye was covered by the shield, and it would publicly shame all Israel. Cutting up the oxen and sending the pieces was a vivid summons to muster, similar to the grim summons in Judges 19. Jabesh-gilead later returns Saul's kindness by rescuing his body, 1 Samuel 31.

Jabesh-gilead already had a history with Benjamin before this siege. A generation earlier, when the other tribes swore to withhold their daughters from the nearly annihilated tribe of Benjamin, the men of Jabesh-gilead were judged for staying home from that assembly, and the young women spared from their town were given to Benjamin's remnant as wives, Judges 21:8-14. A Benjamite king now marches to save the very town bound to his own tribe by that old, uncomfortable debt, though the text never draws the connection out loud.

Saul's tactic, dividing the army into three companies and attacking during the morning watch, follows the same pattern Gideon once used against the Midianites, three companies given horns and torches, a surprise assault timed to the change of the watch, Judges 7:16-19. Seven days of respite before a city's forced surrender, the term Jabesh's elders negotiate, reflects an accepted convention of siege warfare in the period, time enough to seek outside help before capitulating, and Nahash's confident agreement to it shows he expected no rescue to come from a nation he had reason to think was leaderless and divided.
context.canonical:
Saul's Spirit-empowered deliverance stands in the line of the judges God raised up to save Israel, and it develops the book's theme of God saving through His anointed. Naming the victory as the LORD's salvation anticipates the greater salvation of the gospel, and the true King, Jesus, whose name declares that the LORD saves His people from their sins.

Saul's own confession, today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel, verse 13, becomes a refrain the book returns to. When David is later commended for killing Goliath, Jonathan will describe it to Saul in almost the same words, the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel, 1 Samuel 19:5, so that the same formula first spoken by a grateful Saul is later used to defend the very man who will replace him.

An Ammonite king named Nahash resurfaces decades afterward, when David repays a kindness Nahash once showed him by sending comfort to Nahash's son and successor, Hanun, 2 Samuel 10:1-2, a small reminder that the nations pressing on Israel in this chapter do not simply vanish from the story once their siege fails. And the covenant renewal Samuel calls for at Gilgal, verse 14, sets a pattern followed whenever Israel's kingship reaches a crisis point and needs to be publicly reaffirmed before the LORD, as later happens for the boy king Joash, 2 Kings 11:17, and for Josiah, 2 Kings 23:1-3.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
To vindicate Saul's kingship by showing the Spirit-empowered king actually delivering Israel, to credit the salvation to the LORD, and to model humble, God-glorifying leadership before Saul's later decline.

The writer wants the reader who has just heard scoffers ask, how can this man save us, to watch that exact question answered within a single chapter. Saul does save, decisively and completely, the survivors so scattered that no two of them were left together, verse 11, so that the narrative itself functions as the vindication chapter 10 promised was coming. The author is not simply reporting a battle; he is settling an argument the previous chapter left open.

At the same time the writer is training the reader's instincts for how a victory ought to be received. Saul refuses to let the crowd's momentum carry it into an execution of his former critics, and he insists, in the very moment he could most easily have claimed credit, that the LORD, not Saul, worked this salvation. The author intends readers to notice that restraint and to measure every king who comes after, and every reader's own successes, against that same instinct, crediting God rather than settling scores, because that is precisely the instinct Saul himself will abandon in later chapters.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The narrative describes Saul's Spirit-driven rescue and his mercy to critics; it does not prescribe cutting up oxen or waging war as a pattern for believers. What endures is that God works salvation through those He empowers, that victory belongs to the LORD, and that grace, not vengeance, befits the day of God's deliverance.

Nobody is meant to read Saul's dismembered oxen as a template for rallying support, or the three-division night assault as a manual for warfare; those belong to Israel's specific moment as a tribal confederation facing an armed siege, not to believers navigating ordinary conflict now. What does transfer is the pattern beneath the tactics, real crisis met by real, Spirit-given courage, followed by a deliberate choice to let gratitude, not grievance, shape the aftermath of victory. Saul's line, no one shall be put to death this day, is a template worth keeping even where the oxen and the battle plan are not, since believers today face the same temptation to let a hard-won victory become an occasion for settling old scores rather than an occasion for praising the God who gave it.

debates.question: How should we regard Saul in this chapter, given his later failure?

views.label: A genuine high point of Spirit-empowered kingship
views.case: The Spirit really rushed on Saul, God gave a true victory, and Saul rightly credited the LORD and showed mercy; this is authentic good, kingship as God intended, and should be honored as such even in light of what follows.

views.label: A bright beginning that heightens the coming tragedy
views.case: The narrative sets Saul's finest hour early so that his later disobedience and rejection appear all the more sorrowful; the contrast teaches that a gifted, Spirit-touched start is no guarantee of a faithful finish.

debates.bearing: Both are true together: we can honor the real good God did through Saul while learning that empowered beginnings must be matched by persevering obedience, a warning fulfilled positively only in Christ.

debates.question: Why does Saul refuse to punish those who had despised him?

views.label: Humble deflection of glory to God
views.case: Saul insists that today the LORD has worked salvation, so the day belongs to God's mercy, not to settling personal scores; he shows the right instinct that God's deliverance should produce gratitude, not vengeance.

views.label: Political wisdom that unites the nation
views.case: By sparing his critics at the height of his popularity, Saul unites Israel around the throne and the renewal at Gilgal, a magnanimity that consolidates the kingdom without bloodshed.

debates.bearing: Either way Saul's restraint models grace in the hour of triumph, faintly reflecting the greater King who, in His victory, forgives His enemies and saves them.

study.originalLanguages:
Saul's reaction to the messengers' report comes in a precise order worth noticing, first the ruach, the Spirit of God, rushes upon him, and only then does he burn with great anger, verse 6. The verb for burning anger, charah, is common Hebrew vocabulary for kindled wrath, used of Cain, whose countenance fell in anger when his offering was rejected, Genesis 4:5, and of the LORD's own anger kindled against His people's complaints, Numbers 11:1. What makes Saul's anger different from ordinary human rage is its order, the Spirit comes first, and the anger that follows is Spirit-shaped indignation at cruelty rather than a private grievance simply boiling over on its own account.

The pachad that then falls on the people is a specific kind of fear, sudden dread or panic, not the settled, worshipful yare, reverent fear, that Samuel will later demand of Israel in the very next chapter. Pachad is the same word for the great terror and darkness that suddenly overwhelmed Abram as the sun was setting, Genesis 15:12, and for the terror and dread that fell on Israel's own enemies at the Red Sea, Exodus 15:16. Here the same visceral, overwhelming dread is turned toward a good end, uniting Israel for rescue rather than scattering it in despair, showing that God can use even a fear that grips the body before it ever convinces the mind, working through raw instinct exactly as readily as through settled conviction.

Saul's word for what has happened, teshuah, salvation, shares its root with yasha, to save, the very root that gives the Old Testament its ordinary word for deliverance and gives the New Testament, through the name built on that root, the name of Jesus Himself, Matthew 1:21. Saul could have called this day a victory for himself, using a word that would have made the credit his own; he instead reaches for the vocabulary Israel had always reserved for what only God does, and in choosing that word over any word of personal triumph, he unknowingly borrows the very term the New Testament will one day use, in full and without qualification, of the Christ who is still centuries away from being born.

typology.type: The Spirit-empowered king who saves his people
typology.fulfillment: The Spirit does not merely inform Saul of the crisis, it rushes upon him and turns his hearing of bad news into decisive rescue within a single day. Jesus announces His own mission in almost identical terms, the Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor, Luke 4:18, but where Saul's Spirit-driven rescue reaches one town for one day, Christ's Spirit-anointed mission reaches every captive who calls on Him, and unlike Saul's, it never has to be repeated.

typology.type: The rescue of the doomed under threat of the enemy
typology.fulfillment: Jabesh-gilead faces a demand designed to maim and humiliate an entire people, and deliverance arrives only just before the deadline, by the time the sun is hot, verse 9. Paul describes every believer as once threatened by a far graver enemy, rescued from the dominion of darkness and brought into the kingdom of God's beloved Son, Colossians 1:13-14. The type is genuine, a doomed people saved just in time, but the rescue at Jabesh only postpones death, while the rescue in Christ ends it.

typology.type: The victorious king who spares his enemies
typology.fulfillment: At the height of Israel's enthusiasm for killing Saul's former doubters, Saul intervenes, no one shall be put to death this day. Jesus, at the actual height of His own suffering, goes further still, praying over the men driving nails into His hands, Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing, Luke 23:34. Saul spares men who had merely despised him before his victory; Christ forgives men who are killing Him in the very moment of His own.

study.christ:
Saul hears of Jabesh's suffering while walking behind his own oxen, an ordinary man interrupted by an extraordinary need, and the Spirit that rushes on him turns that interruption into a nationwide rescue within a single day. Jesus opens His ministry by reading from Isaiah in His hometown synagogue and applying the words to Himself on the spot, the Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor, He has sent Me to proclaim liberty to the captives, Luke 4:18. Saul's Spirit comes upon him once, for one crisis, and can be withdrawn; Christ carries the Spirit as His constant possession and mission from the very first sentence He preaches.

The threat Saul answers, mutilation and public shame for an entire town, is a small, local shadow of a far larger captivity. Paul tells the Colossians that God has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins, Colossians 1:13-14, language that reframes Jabesh's siege as a picture in miniature of the whole human predicament, besieged by an enemy who intends nothing but harm, until a deliverer comes in time.

But it is Saul's mercy, not his military skill, that reaches furthest toward Christ. On the day of his own triumph he refuses to let anyone die, insisting that the LORD, not personal grievance, be allowed the last word. Jesus goes immeasurably further. He does not simply spare His critics at the height of His success, He forgives the men taking His life at the very moment of His apparent defeat, Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing, Luke 23:34, and turns what looks like His lowest hour into the very salvation Saul could only announce for a single town. What Saul called salvation lasted a season; what Christ accomplished at the cross the New Testament calls the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him, Hebrews 5:9.
study.god:
God's rescue of Jabesh-gilead begins before Saul has any plan of his own; the Spirit simply comes upon him, and courage and clarity of purpose arrive as a gift rather than as the product of Saul's own resolve. This is a God who does not wait to be invited into a crisis by a properly worded appeal; He moves first, and the man He moves is still walking behind his oxen when it happens.

He is a God who can turn even sudden, overwhelming dread into a means of unity rather than despair. The panic that falls on Israel at Saul's grim summons is a visceral kind of fear, the same sort that gripped Abram in the dark and Egypt's army at the sea, yet here it produces exactly the opposite of paralysis, a whole nation rallying as one man to a rescue they had every reason to think was hopeless.

He is precise and complete in judgment when judgment is called for. The Ammonites are not merely repelled, they are scattered so thoroughly that no two of them were left together, verse 11, a totality of victory that leaves no room to credit luck or half measures. When God delivers, He does not deliver halfway.

He is also, in this chapter, the God whose honor Saul instinctively protects even before anyone teaches him to. When the crowd wants blood, Saul reaches for God's reputation rather than his own, insisting that this day belongs to the LORD's salvation, not to any settling of scores, and the narrative lets that instinct stand as the right one without needing to spell out why.

And He is patient with a king He knows will eventually fail Him. This chapter gives Saul his best day, full cooperation with the Spirit, full credit given to God, full restraint toward enemies, and God receives it, confirms the kingship at Gilgal, and lets Israel rejoice greatly, even though the same God already knows, and the reader will soon learn, how briefly this obedience will last. Grace does not wait for a guarantee of permanence before it gives a real and joyful day.

crossReferences.note: The Spirit of the LORD clothed Gideon, the same rushing empowerment that comes on Saul here, both men called from ordinary farm work, one from threshing wheat in a winepress, one from walking behind oxen, to become the rescuer of a threatened Israel.

Stand firm and see the salvation of the LORD, Moses tells a terrified Israel at the sea. Saul echoes the same conviction generations later, refusing to let the day of victory become a day of revenge, because, as he puts it, today the LORD has worked salvation in Israel.

Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing. Christ's prayer for the men killing Him is the far greater fulfillment of the restraint Saul shows toward mere critics on his day of triumph, forgiveness offered not after victory but in the very act of dying.

The angel tells Joseph to name Mary's son Jesus, because of the rescue that name itself carries. The word Saul reaches for at Jabesh, salvation, shares that same root, though Saul's rescue reached one town for a single day and the Son's reaches every believer permanently.

The Spirit of the Lord is on Me, because He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor. Jesus announces at the start of His ministry the very pattern, Spirit first, then rescue, that marks Saul's best day as king.

God has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son. Jabesh-gilead's rescue from a cruel and mutilating enemy becomes a small picture of a far larger deliverance, from an enemy that threatens not an eye but a soul.

The men of Jabesh-gilead had been judged a generation earlier for failing to join Israel's assembly against Benjamin, and the young women spared from their town were given as wives to Benjamin's decimated remnant. A Benjamite king now risks everything to rescue the very town bound to his own tribe by that old, uncomfortable history.

Gideon divides his men into three companies and attacks the Midianite camp by surprise, a tactic Saul repeats almost exactly against the Ammonites, three divisions, a dawn assault, and a rout that scatters the enemy. Israel's deliverers keep learning the same lessons from each other.

Jonathan later defends David to Saul by reminding him that the LORD worked a great salvation for all Israel through him, echoing the very words Saul once used of his own triumph at Jabesh. The formula that first defended Saul's kingship is later used to defend the man who will replace him.

study.oneStory:
Every deliverance in Israel's story answers the same ruined world the fall first produced, a people who cannot save themselves from enemies outside or from the sin inside, and who need God to raise up someone to stand in the gap. Jabesh-gilead's plight is that ruin in miniature, a whole town facing mutilation and shame because it has no strength of its own to resist, and its rescue follows the exact shape every rescue before it has followed since Eden's first promise of a serpent-crushing seed, help coming from outside the sufferers, not from within them.

The chapter also marks a real turning point in how that help arrives. For generations God raised up judges one at a time, as each crisis demanded, but here that same Spirit-driven rescue is performed by a king, folding the office of deliverer into the office of ruler for the first time. It is a genuine advance, and Saul is genuinely good at it on this particular day, but it is not yet the final form the story is reaching for, since a king who can lose the Spirit that empowers him is still, at bottom, only a better version of the same temporary arrangement the judges provided.

The generosity Saul shows at the end of the chapter, refusing vengeance, naming the victory as God's, is the one note in this episode that reaches furthest forward, because it describes exactly the character the story is waiting for its true King to have in full and without failure. Centuries later that King will not merely spare people who doubted Him, He will bear their guilt Himself and rise to offer them an eternal salvation, the very word Saul first reached for at Jabesh, now filled with a weight one town's rescue could never carry, Hebrews 5:9. The story that begins with a besieged town ends with a Savior who besieges no one and rescues everyone who calls on His name.

quiz.q: What cruel condition did Nahash the Ammonite demand of Jabesh-gilead?

options.text: To gouge out every man's right eye, bringing reproach on all Israel.
options.note: Verse 2; the humiliating terms were meant to shame the whole nation.

options.text: That the men of Jabesh become his servants.
options.note: They offered to serve, but Nahash's added condition was to put out every right eye.

options.text: That Jabesh pay him a yearly tribute of gold.
options.note: The demand was the mutilation of every right eye, not tribute.

options.text: That Jabesh give him their finest soldiers.
options.note: His condition was to blind them in one eye, not conscript soldiers.

quiz.q: What moved Saul to rescue Jabesh-gilead?

options.text: The Spirit of God rushed upon him, and he rallied Israel to deliver the city.
options.note: Verse 6; the deliverance began with the Spirit empowering the king, as with the judges.

options.text: Saul burned with anger when he heard of the threat.
options.note: True, but the anger itself followed the Spirit of God rushing upon him.

options.text: Samuel commanded Saul to go to war.
options.note: The Spirit moved Saul directly; Samuel is summoned to march, not the initiator here.

options.text: Saul wanted to prove himself to those who doubted him.
options.note: The text credits the Spirit of God and, afterward, Saul deflects glory to the LORD.

quiz.q: How did Saul respond when the people wanted to kill those who had doubted him?

options.text: He refused, saying no one should die, for that day the LORD had worked salvation in Israel.
options.note: Verse 13; Saul gave God the glory and showed mercy instead of vengeance.

options.text: He spared the men rather than putting them to death.
options.note: True, but omits his reason, that the LORD had worked the salvation, which is the heart of it.

options.text: He agreed to have the doubters executed.
options.note: The opposite; Saul refused to allow any executions.

options.text: He ignored the people and said nothing.
options.note: He spoke clearly, forbidding any deaths and crediting the LORD.

quiz.q: Who does the chapter credit for the deliverance of Jabesh?

options.text: The LORD, who empowered Saul by His Spirit and worked the salvation.
options.note: The Spirit, the terror of the LORD, and Saul's own words all credit God.

options.text: Saul, whose leadership organized and won the battle.
options.note: Saul led, but the text and Saul himself credit the LORD for the salvation.

options.text: The 300,000 soldiers of Israel who fought bravely.
options.note: The army fought, but the deliverance is attributed to God, who rallied and empowered them.

options.text: The elders of Jabesh, who devised a clever plan.
options.note: The rescue came from God through Saul, not from a plan of the elders.

quiz.q: How does Saul's deliverance of Jabesh point forward to Christ?

options.text: As a Spirit-empowered king who works salvation and spares his enemies, he foreshadows Christ, whose name means the LORD saves.
options.note: Saul's partial, passing salvation points to Christ's full and lasting salvation, Matthew 1:21.

options.text: He shows that God rescues His people through leaders He empowers.
options.note: True, but stops short of Christ, the true saving King the chapter anticipates.

options.text: He proves that a good beginning guarantees a faithful life.
options.note: Saul's later failure shows the opposite; only Christ perfectly perseveres.

options.text: He has no connection to Christ.
options.note: The Spirit-empowered saving king clearly foreshadows Jesus.

questions: The rescue of Jabesh began when the Spirit of God moved Saul to act. Where is God stirring you to step into a need rather than staying behind your own plow?
Saul gave God the glory, saying the LORD has worked salvation. When something goes well for you, is your first instinct to credit God or to take the praise yourself?
In his hour of triumph Saul spared those who had despised him. Is there someone who wronged or doubted you whom God is calling you to forgive rather than repay?
Israel rallied when the terror of the LORD fell on them. What would it look like for a right and holy fear of God to move you and your community to action?
Saul's salvation was real but partial; Christ's is complete and lasting. How does resting in the finished salvation of Jesus free you from fear of your true enemies?

translationNotes.note: The BSB notes that the Dead Sea Scrolls and Septuagint read About a month later Nahash, and a longer scroll passage gives background to the siege; the main text follows the shorter Hebrew reading.
The terror of the LORD, pachad, fell on the people, crediting Israel's swift, united response to God, not merely to fear of Saul's grim summons.
The numbers 300,000 and 30,000 follow the Hebrew; the BSB footnote notes the Dead Sea Scrolls and Septuagint read 70,000 men of Judah.
